« Les immigrants sont toujours très part: “Immigrants are always up for a celebration!”
Les membres des communautés sud-asiatiqu: Members of the neighbourhood’s South Asian communities are the volunteers behind the July 1 festivities in Parc-Extension.
Parc-Extension et Montréal-Nord, deux qu: Parc-Extension and Montréal-Nord, two Montréal neighbourhoods known for their rich multicultural fabric, are rarely in the spotlight when it comes to celebrating Quebec’s and Canada’s national holidays. Each takes on different colours for these two occasions. La Converse went behind the scenes of these celebrations to explore festivities dressed sometimes in blue, sometimes in red and white. We wanted to understand what these holidays mean to the immigrants who live in these neighbourhoods, and how they make them their own.
Au milieu de la chaleur de l’après-midi,: In the heat of the afternoon, a few days before Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day, people stand in the shade of the trees in Parc Saint-Roch, tucked at the edge of Parc-Extension beside the railway. A train goes by, then the crossing alarm sounds. One of the women there, Rehana, is taking a well-deserved breath of fresh air during her lunch hour. She has lived in Quebec for six years and lives in the neighbourhood with her husband. She likes Parc-Extension for its tranquility, its range of activities and its local services. “I really like Parc-Extension, I like Quebec too. I take French classes at William-Hingston. Before, I didn’t understand French. I don’t speak much, just a little,” she says with a smile and a proud look. “I’ve improved a lot,” she adds, listing the names of the various teachers to whom she owes her progress.
Rehana, une résidente de Parc-Extension,: Rehana, a Parc-Extension resident, takes French-language classes a stone’s throw from Parc Saint-Roch. Photo: Khady Konaté
Cela fait bientôt deux ans que la cinqua: For almost two years now, the woman in her fifties, who is originally from South Africa, has been taking French classes at the adult education school located right next to the park. Among other things, she has learned a few songs from the French-language and Quebec repertoire, and she watches television and listens to the radio in the language of Molière. Yet when we ask her about taking part in the Saint-Jean festivities, she doesn’t seem to know what they are. After a moment of thought, she says: “I don’t know it, no. But they explained it to us a little in our classes,” she adds before walking away.
<strong>Parc-Extension, un quartier qui: Parc-Extension, a neighbourhood that doesn’t celebrate Saint-Jean
À Parc-Extension, contrairement à la maj: In Parc-Extension, unlike most neighbourhoods in the city, no citizens’ group organizes festivities to mark Quebec’s Fête nationale. The neighbourhood, which stands out for its cultural mosaic, is one of the most multicultural in Montréal. Its main communities are Greek, Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi. According to the territorial analysis carried out by Centraide in 2020-2021, it welcomes more newcomers than the Montréal average. In total, 69% of its residents have a mother tongue other than English or French, and 90% of its residents are first- or second-generation immigrants. Densely populated, it is also one of the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods in Canada: according to Centraide, 38% of its population lives on a low income.
De l’avis de l’ancienne mairesse de l’ar: In the view of Giuliana Fumagalli, former mayor of the Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension borough, these characteristics must be taken into account to understand the absence of Saint-Jean celebrations in Parc-Extension. “There are structural elements in the neighbourhood that mean people don’t necessarily have the time. There are Québécois in the neighbourhood – I live here myself – but nobody does it. It takes someone.”
Pour l’ancienne élue, la question dépass: For the former elected official, the question goes beyond a sense of belonging to the province. She recalls the festivities held in Villeray, the neighbouring area, where immigrant families from Parc-Extension would join in. “Immigrants are always up for a celebration!” she points out. However, there is an elephant in the room: the lack of representation of cultural communities in Saint-Jean celebrations. According to Ms. Fumagalli, artists from immigrant backgrounds are too rarely on stage and are not approached enough to take part in the activities. Very close to artists from cultural diversity, she can attest to how little attention the festivities’ organizers pay to the borough’s talent, despite how deeply rooted these artists are in Québécois culture. She considers it a missed opportunity, because “if we invite them, people will come – people are just waiting for that!” It makes you wonder, she says, “what it takes to be Québécois.” “The lack of representation in the cultural sector is part of the problem. You only have to look at the youth here, it’s not talent that’s missing. The young people, they’re Montrealers, deeply Montrealers, and they don’t see themselves represented,” says the woman, who remains active in her community.
À l’instar de sa prédécesseure, l’actuel: Like her predecessor, the current borough mayor, Laurence Lavigne-Lalonde, reports that the neighbourhood’s communities do have a taste for celebrating, but that they mobilize more for the national holidays of their countries of origin. Although she does not come from an immigrant background, she understands that it can be important for people from different diasporas to celebrate their culture surrounded by their own. But also to be able to share it with their host society and the other communities they live alongside, in order to show its richness. “Events like these help strengthen solidarity between communities, in addition to contributing to living together and taking people on a journey for a day.”
Mme Lavigne-Lalonde souligne toutefois q: Ms. Lavigne-Lalonde points out, however, that in everyday life, once the festivities are over, this coexistence is undermined by the recent adoption of Bill 96. The law requires government, municipal and public service employees to serve users in French. “I think it’s really an obstacle to inclusion and living together. If we want people to feel welcome and to develop an affinity with the host language, we first have to be able to welcome them in a language they understand, so we can communicate better, guide them and make them want to learn French. (…) I’m thinking of the parent who has to register their child at school, or the adult who wants help entering the job market and who learned English before immigrating… It’s really a challenge.” On the ground, she says she is working with partners to help those who need it overcome the language barrier. “We have no choice,” says the mayor.
Si rien n’y est prévu pour la Fête natio: While nothing is planned for the Fête nationale, Parc-Extension is on the other hand the only neighbourhood in Montréal to hold Canada Day celebrations – with the exception of the Pierrefonds-Roxboro borough. Next to Parc metro station, Place de la Gare is draped in red and white for the occasion. The event, organized by the Conseil national bangladeshi-canadien, mostly brings together members of the neighbourhood’s South Asian communities.
Malgré la pluie, les bénévoles s’activen: Despite the rain, volunteers are busy with the final preparations for the event. Photo: Khady Konaté
Portant des chandails rouges et brandiss: Wearing red shirts and waving flags, women apply temporary maple leaf tattoos to their cheeks. Children run around and eye the table where a cake takes pride of place. Farther along, men, a few of them wearing turbans, bustle around the barbecue and prepare plates for the free meal distribution. Dhols and traditional Punjabi music resound. On the stage set up for the occasion, musicians follow one another with bhangra dancers, who in turn get the ever-growing crowd swaying its hips. Unique, the atmosphere skilfully blends the cultural heritage of the communities present with a Canadian flavour.
Les résidents ont servi du gâteau pour s: Residents served cake to mark Canada Day. Photo: Shahista Hussein
Nandini Gupta, une jeune femme de 17 ans: Nandini Gupta, a 17-year-old young woman, is taking part in the festivities. She is proud to mark Canada Day with her family and members of her community. She has lived in Quebec for five years. For her, celebrating is a way of showing gratitude to the country that took her in. Having had to leave India with her family following problems she does not specify, Nandini believes that “the government helped us a lot on our journey, it saved us.” That is also why, she says, members of her community are here. Like many of the neighbourhood’s residents, Nandini and her family are waiting for a decision on their asylum claim in Canada. She believes the government can help them again by granting permanent residency, to her and to others taking part in the Canada Day celebrations. For her, it is an exchange: “We give to Canada, and Canada gives [back] to us.”
Nandini Gupta est une jeune femme de 17: Nandini Gupta is a 17-year-old young woman taking part in Canada Day in Parc-Extension. Photo: Khady Konaté
La jeune femme, qui aimerait devenir tra: The young woman, who would like to become a social worker, is already supporting her community. “Me, I’ve always volunteered, and I’ve met all these people. Even though I’m in the same situation as they are, I try to help them, because they don’t speak French. If they need translation, I’ll do it; especially if it’s to help them move forward on their journey […] I see all the effort they put in. I’m very hopeful that everyone will have their papers in the short term.” Despite her confident tone, Nandini says that several families have been deported in recent months. Although it is a time for celebration at Place de la Gare, a shadow hangs over some families in the neighbourhood.
<strong>Montréal-Nord et sa multitude de: Montréal-Nord and its multitude of blue-and-white celebrations
Montréal-Nord, qui est trois fois plus p: Montréal-Nord, which has three times the population of Parc-Extension, is a neighbourhood on the island of Montréal that rivals the latter in cultural diversity. However, when it comes to June 24 festivities, Montréal-Nord stands out for its multitude of activities, enough to shatter some preconceived ideas. Asked about the festivities organized by the borough and community partners – the initiative came from the Société d’histoire et de généalogie de Montréal-Nord – Abdelhaq Sari, city councillor for Montréal-Nord, exclaims: “Honestly, I really enjoyed it! There was an extraordinary multicultural presence.” Since his election in the Marie-Clarac district in 2017, he does not recall seeing so many immigrants and racialized people join the celebration. On the programme: two days of activities, with face painting, games, fireworks, shows and a concert by singer Annie Villeneuve at Parc Aimé-Léonard. “Seeing people sing her lyrics along with her, that’s really something. […] It’s not your date of arrival that makes you more Québécois than anyone else.”
Le conseiller rappelle qu’en plus de la: The councillor points out that, in addition to the official local celebration, several other activities took place on a smaller scale. The Ach-Choura cultural centre and the Ahmadiyya mosque also invited the community to mark Saint-Jean.
« Malheureusement, quand ce genre d’acti: “Unfortunately, when this kind of activity takes place in Montréal-Nord, nobody is interested,” laments Mr. Sari. Stereotypes about the neighbourhood are persistent, particularly those about young people, which never fails to irritate the councillor. Despite efforts to boost the leisure offerings, Montréal-Nord is still waiting for its sports centre, and the lack of facilities is felt, he says. “Young people take part in activities; they are our next generation and we take poor care of them. A third of the population is young and from diverse backgrounds. But these young people are poorly served, that’s all,” the councillor repeats.
L’organisme Hoodstock a également offert: The organization Hoodstock also offered residents of the Nord-Est sector a festive activity by holding the fourth edition of its Festihood. Founded in 2020, the festival was born while Montréal-Nord was the Canadian epicentre of COVID-19. Dalila Awada, the organization’s public relations manager, remembers that the community’s morale was at rock bottom then, and the atmosphere “stressful and unpleasant.” “The first goal was really to bring life, to bring joy, colour,” explains the Hoodstock representative. The Festihood takes place every year on the same date, June 24. “The idea is to mark Saint-Jean, but with a Hoodstock, Montréal-Nord touch. So we celebrate diversity, the creativity of local artists, the solidarity in our area.”
Après une première édition réussie, l’év: After a successful first edition, the event became an annual fixture. It took the form of a parade with a mobile stage: the procession travels through the streets of Montréal-Nord for an afternoon. The performances are by local and emerging artists, who sometimes get the chance to take their first steps in front of an audience there. Alongside this, in collaboration with La Tablée des Chefs, Hoodstock distributes meals to residents using surplus food recovered from restaurants. This year, the parade was cancelled because of the risk of thunderstorms, but 10,000 meals were served by the organization’s team and a handful of volunteers.
Selon notre interlocutrice, la parade es: According to our interviewee, the parade is more accessible than other events. Indeed, mobility and precarity issues make it easier to go out and celebrate in the street, where residents can take part in the activity from their balconies. “People won’t necessarily travel to take part in Saint-Jean activities in other, more central neighbourhoods or go see big shows; the idea is to offer them, at home, a little something that looks like them.” Residents can enjoy performances by music groups and traditional dance troupes, such as the group Rara Soley. “It lets them recognize themselves in the more traditional aspects of their culture,” explains Dalila.
Au Pavillon du parc Henri-Bourassa, par: At the pavilion in Parc Henri-Bourassa, on a rainy afternoon, we meet Salomon Loussaint, a Montréal-Nord resident. His face is calm, and he smiles discreetly. His soft, measured voice invites conversation. You quickly gather that he is used to human contact, as he works as a youth worker in local schools. Seated at a table with two girls who will start high school next year, Salomon is busy stimulating their minds with the educational game Mots Rapido.
Né à Montréal-Nord de parents haïtiens,: Born in Montréal-Nord to Haitian parents, the 26-year-old is firmly rooted in the neighbourhood. He grew up there and has never left. Yet, as far back as he can remember, he has never celebrated Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day or Canada Day. “We didn’t go to those kinds of parties or events,” he says bluntly. His parents simply weren’t in the mood for it. That was the case for many immigrant parents, he says. It has stayed with him, especially since he doesn’t much like big crowds. With age, however, Salomon began to depart from the family tradition, joining Saint-Jean celebrations a few times with friends. “Alone, I’ll rarely go, but if it’s with a group of friends, I’m more likely to go,” says the man himself.
Salomon Loussaint, au pavillon du parc H: Salomon Loussaint, at the pavilion in Parc Henri-Bourassa in Montréal-Nord. Photo: Khady Konaté
Lorsqu’on lui demande s’il éprouve de l’: When asked whether he feels attached to the province or the country, he hesitates for a moment, then answers: “Well, for sure there’s some, because I was born here. It’s also the land that welcomed my parents and my grandparents… But there’s no more attachment than that. I know I was born in Quebec, I’m Québécois yes, but… Saint-Jean-Baptiste, it’s not a holiday I’m going to go celebrate on my own,” he says, before adding: “I feel Canadian, but nothing more.”
En revanche, Salomon se dit très fier d’: On the other hand, Salomon says he is very proud to be Haitian. “The older I get, the more I learn about my culture, and the more I learn to be proud of my country […] It’s a way of learning who I am, in a way.” The young man explains how the historical stories surrounding Haitian Flag Day and joumou soup, a traditional dish served on Independence Day, have allowed him to appreciate his heritage even more.
Parler de double identité le laisse pens: Talking about a dual identity leaves him pensive. He takes the time to choose his words. “I think we have no choice, when we talk about Haitian roots and Québécois roots, but to talk about systemic racism… or even the history of slavery that existed in Quebec.” As a young Black man born and living in Montréal-Nord, labels and stereotypes stick to him. Clichés he vigorously rejects. “Lately, I’ve taken a lot of pride in being a Black man, being a Black father, being a Black husband.” Active in his community in sports and education since his teens, Salomon is committed to having a positive impact wherever he goes. He enjoys defying expectations and surpassing himself, just like professional athletes Bennedict Mathurin and Luguentz Dort, who come from Montréal-Nord and are role models for him. On the negative images conveyed about his neighbourhood, Salomon exclaims: “I like it, I’d say, being the underdog! (…) For me, I think it’s important to be proud of where you come from, no matter the neighbourhood. Me, I’m really proud to be from Montréal-Nord,” concludes the man whose sense of belonging to the neighbourhood runs deep.
